summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This conversation is a direct continuation of an ongoing technical project in which Claude is performing a systematic Phase R2 review of a multi-volume academic work called "The Method 1.6." The person is orchestrating a structured review workflow using a handoff document system (HANDOFF-26 → HANDOFF-27) across multiple chat sessions. The work involves reading specific line ranges of the main volume against cited sections, the Register, and the Mathematical Compendium, then re-measuring every tower-computable claim using Python instruments that load a constraint tower (tower-2.py) through a shared library (r2lib.py).

Chat 75 completed five segments covering sections §12.11.0.8 through §12.11.0.12, completing the entire §12.11.0 block. Each segment followed a strict protocol: run clerical checkers (r2-tools.py) on the line range, read every line, resolve all pointers to headings and claims, write a Python instrument (r2-ch12l.py through r2-ch12p.py) importing r2lib by path, run it on all cells or pairs, bank the golden output, and produce a READ file and CENSUS-CLOSURES file before moving to the next segment. Four findings for the future R3 revision pass were identified: 12l-01 (a flawed proof route claiming treewidth 2 gives only an envelope, refuted by the tower's own cycle row closing exactly), 12l-02 ("independent sources" that are actually statistically dependent), 12m-01 (a sign-extension claim with no recoverable population), and 12o-01 (the word "surplus" naming two different quantities across sections). The session closed by building BUILD102 (3,301,547 B · md5 2e47effae1c96afec1804c3ab5bd03da) from BUILD101 by appending W-112, a DEFERRED block, and twenty new members, then writing HANDOFF-27 for chat 76 to continue at §12.11.1.

The project enforces strict discipline: instruments must be deterministic (no wall-clock output), pycaches must be deleted after every run, segments must be fully closed before the next opens, lowercase "register NNN" pointers are missed by r2-tools' case-sensitive regex and require manual resolution, and the close procedure requires a reverse-recovery guard confirming the new bundle can reconstruct the prior bundle's md5.

**Tool Knowledge**

Google Drive searches used `title contains 'BUILD102_compendia' or title contains 'BUILD90_main'` with `pageSize 5` and `excludeContentSnippets True`; this reliably locates both bundles by title without returning content previews. In chat 75, Drive download spills produced only a one-line pointer in context rather than a ~65 KB preview (as occurred in chat 74), reducing gate context cost to approximately 5%. The bootstrap step decodes spill files from `/mnt/user-data/tool_results/<tool-call-id>.json` using `json.loads(json.load(open(path))[0]['text'])['content']` before base64 decoding with `validate=True`. Python heredocs must not be wrapped in `sh -c '...'` due to quoting breakage in dash shell; each heredoc requires its own bash tool call. The `gate.py manifest` command locates the compendia bundle by scanning `/home/claude` for one `BUILD*_compendia` file, so if two are present after a close, `--comp <path>` must be passed explicitly.

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312

  2843	 §10.2 reads the constraint tree as past — change — future. **That reading has arithmetic, and it is
  2844	 not the arithmetic of three free things.**
  2845	
  2846	 **Treated as independent the three parts overcount by 130%**: |A|·|Q|·|B| = 33 · 4 · 17 = 2,244
  2847	 against |Λ| = 976, a defect of 1,268. Conditioned on the transfer they separate exactly, defect zero.
  2848	
  2849	 **And the balance is not special to the transfer.** Every two-sided cut of the tree gives it —
  2850	 **ℓ, q, f and g, all defect zero.** §12.6.1 presents the factorisation as though the transfer were
  2851	 doing the work; the computation says the *tree* is doing it, and q is distinguished only by which two
  2852	 things it separates.
  2853	
  2854	 **And the reason it is exactly four is the tree.** Deleting a coordinate splits the constraint graph
  2855	 into two components precisely when that coordinate is an internal vertex of degree two. n, e and 2S
  2856	 are leaves and deleting one leaves a single component; k has degree three and deleting it leaves
  2857	 three. **ℓ, q, f and g are the caterpillar's four internal degree-two vertices, and they are the
  2858	 only two-sided cuts that exist.** Recomputed on the tree rather than on coordinate order: defect
  2859	 zero at every one of the four, and the other four are not two-sided cuts at all. The list was
  2860	 complete when it was written and never said why. Register 408.
  2861	
  2862	 **The shape is a path.** Two edges, past ↔ present and present ↔ future, and no past–future edge —
  2863	 treewidth 1. By §18.4.1 treewidth 1 closes exactly and treewidth 2 gives an envelope, so **Λ's
  2864	 exactness is a proof that the three parts are not a triangle.** A triangle would be the three-body
  2865	 shape and register 316 states its price.
  2866	
  2867	 **The future is never a value.** Of **97** (past, present) pairs, **none determines a single future** —
  2868	 futures per pair run 5, median 10, maximum 17. And for each value of the present, **every past gives
  2869	 the same future set**:

### 12.11.0.8 Past, present and future — a path, not a triangle
 §10.2 reads the constraint tree as past — change — future. **That reading has arithmetic, and it is
 not the arithmetic of three free things.**

 **Treated as independent the three parts overcount by 130%**: |A|·|Q|·|B| = 33 · 4 · 17 = 2,244
 against |Λ| = 976, a defect of 1,268. Conditioned on the transfer they separate exactly, defect zero.

 **And the balance is not special to the transfer.** Every two-sided cut of the tree gives it —
 **ℓ, q, f and g, all defect zero.** §12.6.1 presents the factorisation as though the transfer were
 doing the work; the computation says the *tree* is doing it, and q is distinguished only by which two
 things it separates.

 **And the reason it is exactly four is the tree.** Deleting a coordinate splits the constraint graph
 into two components precisely when that coordinate is an internal vertex of degree two. n, e and 2S
 are leaves and deleting one leaves a single component; k has degree three and deleting it leaves
 three. **ℓ, q, f and g are the caterpillar's four internal degree-two vertices, and they are the
 only two-sided cuts that exist.** Recomputed on the tree rather than on coordinate order: defect
 zero at every one of the four, and the other four are not two-sided cuts at all. The list was
 complete when it was written and never said why. Register 408.

 **The shape is a path.** Two edges, past ↔ present and present ↔ future, and no past–future edge —
 treewidth 1. By §18.4.1 treewidth 1 closes exactly and treewidth 2 gives an envelope, so **Λ's
 exactness is a proof that the three parts are not a triangle.** A triangle would be the three-body
 shape and register 316 states its price.

 **The future is never a value.** Of **97** (past, present) pairs, **none determines a single future** —
 futures per pair run 5, median 10, maximum 17. And for each value of the present, **every past gives
 the same future set**:

  present q     distinct pasts    distinct future sets    |future|
  0                        33                       1            5
  1                        33                       1           10
  2                        23                       1           15
  3                         8                       1           17

    **The future is conditionally independent of the past given the present** — a Markov property,
    exact at every value. The past constrains only which presents are reachable; having spent that,
    it has spent everything.

 The dependence is monotone and opposed: the future set nests increasing, 5 ⊂ 10 ⊂ 15 ⊂ 17, while the
 past set nests decreasing, 33 ⊇ 33 ⊇ 23 ⊇ 8. **And the bracket is saturated** — at every present the
 admissible future is the full interval between its own extremes, nothing inside missing. E(X) = 0 read
 on the target end.

 **The tick, decomposed.** Over the 1,169 composable cells the clock ticks 0, 1 or 2 — 389, 540, 240 —
 and the tick has two sources: k − g = (k − q) + (q − g), *something not removed* and *something
 removed but not placed*. **350 against 350 pure, with 80 cells in both**, and the split table is its own transpose: (0,1) = 270
 against (1,0) = 270, (0,2) = 80 against (2,0) = 80.

    **Irreversibility has two independent sources contributing identically.** One is a choice not
    taken; the other a capacity that could not receive. The index weights them the same.

 **And Pauli is a minority partner in it.** g's ceiling is fixed by counting in 60.2% of composable
 cells, tied in 29.5%, and by shell capacity in only 10.3%. **The arrow of time in this object is
 overwhelmingly a counting phenomenon**, which §12.9 states in advance. Register 357.

input.file_text:
# r2-ch12l.py — Phase R2, main §12.11.0.8 "Past, present and future — a path, not a triangle" (L2842–2897), chat 75.
# Every tower-computable claim of the section re-measured on ALL 976 cells of Λ₈ and ALL 1,654 cells of Λ₉ (tower-2.py by path
# through r2lib.load_tower); constraint tree of Λ₈ = r2lib.EDGES9 without the 2S′ edge; composable cells as r2-ch12e/f define them
# (a cell whose target (e,f,g,2S′) is a source object (n,ℓ,k,2S) of some cell). Deterministic; prints no wall-clock time.
import importlib.util, os, statistics, itertools
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
H = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
s = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('r2lib', os.path.join(H, 'r2lib.py')); r2lib = importlib.util.module_from_spec(s); s.loader.exec_module(r2lib); T = r2lib.load_tower()

L8 = T.L8(); L9 = T.L9()
N8 = ['n', 'ℓ', 'k', 'q', 'e', 'f', 'g', '2S']
A_IDX, Q_IDX, B_IDX = (0, 1, 2, 7), 3, (4, 5, 6)               # past (source), present (transfer), future (target) on Λ₈
EDGES8 = [e for e in r2lib.EDGES9 if 8 not in e]                # Λ₈'s constraint tree: 7 edges on 8 coordinates
proj = lambda c, idx: tuple(c[i] for i in idx)

print(f'|Λ8| {len(L8):,} | |Λ9| {len(L9):,} | tower-2.py L8/L9 by path')

# ---- L2846–2847: the three parts treated as free, and conditioned on q ----
A = {proj(c, A_IDX) for c in L8}; Qs = {c[Q_IDX] for c in L8}; B = {proj(c, B_IDX) for c in L8}
prod = len(A) * len(Qs) * len(B); defect = prod - len(L8)
Aq = defaultdict(set); Bq = defaultdict(set)
for c in L8: Aq[c[Q_IDX]].add(proj(c, A_IDX)); Bq[c[Q_IDX]].add(proj(c, B_IDX))
cond = sum(len(Aq[v]) * len(Bq[v]) for v in Aq) - len(L8)
print(f'== L2846–2847 free parts: |A|(n,ℓ,k,2S) {len(A)} · |Q| {len(Qs)} · |B|(e,f,g) {len(B)} = {prod:,} against |Λ8| {len(L8)}: defect {defect:,} = overcount {100*defect/len(L8):.1f}% | conditioned on q: Σ_q|A_q||B_q| − |Λ8| = {cond}')
print(f'   per q: A_q {[len(Aq[v]) for v in sorted(Aq)]} B_q {[len(Bq[v]) for v in sorted(Bq)]} cross-sections {[len(Aq[v])*len(Bq[v]) for v in sorted(Aq)]} (sum {sum(len(Aq[v])*len(Bq[v]) for v in Aq)})')

# ---- L2849–2860: every two-sided cut; the tree; degrees; the caterpillar ----
print(f'== L2854–2860 constraint tree on Λ8: edges {[(N8[a], N8[b]) for a, b in EDGES8]} | is_tree {r2lib.is_tree(8, EDGES8)}')
deg = Counter(); [deg.update([a, b]) for a, b in EDGES8]
leaves = [N8[i] for i in range(8) if deg[i] == 1]
spine_edges = [(a, b) for a, b in EDGES8 if deg[a] > 1 and deg[b] > 1]
print(f'   degrees {[(N8[i], deg[i]) for i in range(8)]} | leaves {leaves} | leaves removed leaves a path (caterpillar): {r2lib.is_tree(len({v for e in spine_edges for v in e}), [(sorted({v for e in spine_edges for v in e}).index(a), sorted({v for e in spine_edges for v in e}).index(b)) for a, b in spine_edges]) and all(sum(1 for a, b in spine_edges if v in (a, b)) <= 2 for e in spine_edges for v in e)}')
def cut_defect(cells, c, S1, S2):
    P = defaultdict(set); R = defaultdict(set)
    for x in cells: P[x[c]].add(proj(x, S1)); R[x[c]].add(proj(x, S2))
    return sum(len(P[v]) * len(R[v]) for v in P) - len(cells)
rows = []
for c in range(8):
    comp = r2lib.components(EDGES8, {c}, nodes=8)
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for v, root in comp.items(): groups[root].append(v)
    parts = sorted(sorted(g) for g in groups.values())
    if len(parts) == 2:
        rows.append(f'{N8[c]}: 2 components {[[N8[i] for i in p] for p in parts]} → tree-cut defect {cut_defect(L8, c, tuple(parts[0]), tuple(parts[1]))}; coordinate-order cut (before | after) defect {cut_defect(L8, c, tuple(range(c)), tuple(range(c+1, 8)))}')
    else:
        rows.append(f'{N8[c]}: {len(parts)} component(s) {[[N8[i] for i in p] for p in parts]} — not a two-sided cut')
print('   ' + '\n   '.join(rows))

# ---- L2862–2865: the quotient on {A, q, B} is a path ----
part = {i: 'A' for i in A_IDX}; part[Q_IDX] = 'Q'; part.update({i: 'B' for i in B_IDX})
qe = Counter(tuple(sorted((part[a], part[b]))) for a, b in EDGES8 if part[a] != part[b])
print(f'== L2862–2863 quotient edges between parts: A–Q {qe[("A","Q")]} ({[(N8[a],N8[b]) for a,b in EDGES8 if {part[a],part[b]}=={"A","Q"}]}), Q–B {qe[("B","Q")]} ({[(N8[a],N8[b]) for a,b in EDGES8 if {part[a],part[b]}=={"B","Q"}]}), A–B {qe[("A","B")]} | path on three vertices (treewidth 1): {qe[("A","Q")]>=1 and qe[("B","Q")]>=1 and qe[("A","B")]==0}')
# the tower's own treewidth-2 index, Λ9′ (cycle f–g–2S′): closure, from r2lib (banked in r2-ch12i)
L9p = r2lib.lam9p(L9)
n2, jl, ml = r2lib.closure(L9p)
tri = [e for e in r2lib.EDGES9P if set(e) <= {5, 6, 8}]
print(f'   Λ9′ (cycle): edges among f, g, 2S′ {len(tri)} (a triangle, treewidth 2) | closure on {n2:,} pairs: join leaves {jl}, meet leaves {ml} — E(Λ9′) = {jl+ml}')

# ---- L2867–2879: (past, present) pairs, futures, the table, Markov ----
fut = defaultdict(set)
for c in L8: fut[(proj(c, A_IDX), c[Q_IDX])].add(proj(c, B_IDX))
sizes = sorted(len(v) for v in fut.values())
print(f'== L2867–2868 (past, present) pairs {len(fut)} | pairs determining a single future {sum(1 for v in fut.values() if len(v)==1)} | futures per pair min {sizes[0]}, median {statistics.median(sizes)}, max {sizes[-1]}')
print('   present q | distinct pasts | distinct future sets | |future|')
for v in sorted(Aq):
    fsets = {frozenset(fut[(a, v)]) for a in Aq[v]}
    print(f'   {v} | {len(Aq[v])} | {len(fsets)} | {sorted(len(f) for f in fsets)}')
cells, fails = r2lib.ci_sets(L8, list(A_IDX), list(B_IDX), [Q_IDX])
print(f'   L2877 exact conditional independence (n,ℓ,k,2S) ⊥ (e,f,g) | q on Λ8: product cells {cells}, count-test failures {fails}')

# ---- L2881–2884: nesting; the saturated bracket; E on the target end ----
vs = sorted(Aq)
fut_nest = all(Bq[vs[i]] < Bq[vs[i+1]] for i in range(len(vs)-1))
past_nest = all(Aq[vs[i]] >= Aq[vs[i+1]] for i in range(len(vs)-1))
print(f'== L2881–2882 future sets nest increasing (strict ⊂) {fut_nest} sizes {[len(Bq[v]) for v in vs]} | past sets nest decreasing (⊇) {past_nest} sizes {[len(Aq[v]) for v in vs]} | A_0 = A_1: {Aq[vs[0]]==Aq[vs[1]]}')
for v in vs:
    S = Bq[v]; lo = tuple(min(b[i] for b in S) for i in range(3)); hi = tuple(max(b[i] for b in S) for i in range(3))
    inB = {b for b in B if all(lo[i] <= b[i] <= hi[i] for i in range(3))}
    box = {b for b in itertools.product(*[range(lo[i], hi[i]+1) for i in range(3)])}
    _, j, m = r2lib.closure(sorted(S))
    print(f'   q = {v}: |B_q| {len(S)} | extremes lo {lo} hi {hi} both in B_q {lo in S and hi in S} | B ∩ [lo,hi] = B_q: {inB == S} ({len(inB)}) | full box [lo,hi] in Z³ {len(box)} (B_q = box: {box == S}) | closure of B_q: join leaves {j}, meet leaves {m}')
_, j, m = r2lib.closure(sorted(B)); print(f'   the 17-element target set B: closure join leaves {j}, meet leaves {m}')

# ---- L2886–2892: the tick over the composable cells of Λ9 ----
O = {r2lib.src(c) for c in L9}
comp = [c for c in L9 if r2lib.tgt(c) in O]
print(f'== L2886 composable cells (target is a source object) {len(comp):,} of {len(L9):,} | = cells with g ≥ 1: {len(comp)==sum(1 for c in L9 if c[6]>=1)} | non-composable {len(L9)-len(comp)}')
tick = Counter(c[2] - c[6] for c in comp)
print(f'   tick k − g over composable cells: {dict(sorted(tick.items()))} | max over ALL Λ9 cells {max(c[2]-c[6] for c in L9)}, min {min(c[2]-c[6] for c in L9)}')
split = Counter((c[2] - c[3], c[3] - c[6]) for c in comp)
print(f'   split (k−q, q−g): {dict(sorted(split.items()))} | table is its own transpose: {all(split[(i,j)]==split[(j,i)] for i in range(3) for j in range(3))}')
pure1 = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i > 0 and j == 0); pure2 = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i == 0 and j > 0); both = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i > 0 and j > 0)
src1 = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i > 0); src2 = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if j > 0)
print(f'   pure k−q>0 only {pure1}, pure q−g>0 only {pure2}, both {both} | any k−q>0 {src1} against any q−g>0 {src2} (Register 357\'s "430 against 430") | tick 1 = (0,1)+(1,0) {split[(0,1)]+split[(1,0)]}, tick 2 = (0,2)+(2,0)+(1,1) {split[(0,2)]+split[(2,0)]+split[(1,1)]}')
# statistical independence of the two sources over the composable cells (L2891 "two independent sources")
N = len(comp); ci_fail = sum(1 for i in range(3) for j in range(3) if split[(i, j)] * N != sum(split[(i, jj)] for jj in range(3)) * sum(split[(ii, j)] for ii in range(3)))
exp11 = sum(split[(1, jj)] for jj in range(3)) * sum(split[(ii, 1)] for ii in range(3)) / N
print(f'   k−q ⊥ q−g on composable cells: exact count test fails on {ci_fail} of 9 cells; N(1,1) {split[(1,1)]} against independence {exp11:.1f}; mutual information {r2lib.mi([c[2]-c[3] for c in comp],[c[3]-c[6] for c in comp]):.3f} bits | marginals equal (identical contribution): {[sum(split[(i,jj)] for jj in range(3)) for i in range(3)]} vs {[sum(split[(ii,j)] for ii in range(3)) for j in range(3)]}')
# the 389 of r2-ch12f: cells on a cycle = cells whose source and target objects lie in one SCC of the object graph
edges = defaultdict(int)
for c in comp: edges[(r2lib.src(c), r2lib.tgt(c))] += 1
adj = defaultdict(list)
for (a, b) in edges: adj[a].append(b)
sccs = r2lib.tarjan(sorted(O), adj); cid = {o: i for i, cp in enumerate(sccs) for o in cp}
cyc = [c for c in comp if cid[r2lib.src(c)] == cid[r2lib.tgt(c)]]
t0 = [c for c in comp if c[2] == c[6]]
rev = sum(1 for (a, b) in edges if (b, a) in edges)
print(f'   cells on a composition cycle (source and target in one SCC; SCCs {len(sccs)}) {len(cyc)} | tick-0 composable cells {len(t0)} | the two sets are identical: {set(cyc)==set(t0)} | object edges with a reverse edge {rev} (r2-ch12f: 389)')

# ---- L2894–2895: g's ceiling min(4f+2, q) over the composable cells ----
ceil = Counter('counting (q < 4f+2)' if c[3] < 4*c[5]+2 else ('tied (q = 4f+2)' if c[3] == 4*c[5]+2 else 'shell capacity (4f+2 < q)') for c in comp)
print(f'== L2894–2895 g\'s ceiling over {len(comp):,} composable cells: ' + ' | '.join(f'{k} {v} = {100*v/len(comp):.1f}%' for k, v in sorted(ceil.items())))
ceil_all = Counter('counting' if c[3] < 4*c[5]+2 else ('tied' if c[3] == 4*c[5]+2 else 'shell') for c in L9)
ceil8 = Counter('counting' if c[3] < 4*c[5]+2 else ('tied' if c[3] == 4*c[5]+2 else 'shell') for c in L8)
print(f'   for comparison — all Λ9 cells: ' + ', '.join(f'{k} {v} ({100*v/len(L9):.1f}%)' for k, v in sorted(ceil_all.items())) + ' | Λ8 cells: ' + ', '.join(f'{k} {v} ({100*v/len(L8):.1f}%)' for k, v in sorted(ceil8.items())))
att = Counter((c[3] < 4*c[5]+2, c[6] == min(4*c[5]+2, c[3])) for c in comp)
print(f'   composable cells at the ceiling (g = min(4f+2, q)): {sum(v for (a, b), v in att.items() if b)} of {len(comp):,}; of those, ceiling by counting {att[(True, True)]}, by capacity or tie {att[(False, True)]}')

Aq = defaultdict(set); Bq = defaultdict(set)

print(f'== L2846–2847 free parts: |A|(n,ℓ,k,2S) {len(A)} · |Q| {len(Qs)} · |B|(e,f,g) {len(B)} = {prod:,} against |Λ8| {len(L8)}: defect {defect:,} = overcount {100*defect/len(L8):.1f}% | conditioned on q: Σ_q|A_q||B_q| − |Λ8| = {cond}')
print(f'   per q: A_q {[len(Aq[v]) for v in sorted(Aq)]} B_q {[len(Bq[v]) for v in sorted(Bq)]} cross-sections {[len(Aq[v])*len(Bq[v]) for v in sorted(Aq)]} (sum {sum(len(Aq[v])*len(Bq[v]) for v in Aq)})')

print(f'== L2854–2860 constraint tree on Λ8: edges {[(N8[a], N8[b]) for a, b in EDGES8]} | is_tree {r2lib.is_tree(8, EDGES8)}')

leaves = [N8[i] for i in range(8) if deg[i] == 1]
spine_edges = [(a, b) for a, b in EDGES8 if deg[a] > 1 and deg[b] > 1]
print(f'   degrees {[(N8[i], deg[i]) for i in range(8)]} | leaves {leaves} | leaves removed leaves a path (caterpillar): {r2lib.is_tree(len({v for e in spine_edges for v in e}), [(sorted({v for e in spine_edges for v in e}).index(a), sorted({v for e in spine_edges for v in e}).index(b)) for a, b in spine_edges]) and all(sum(1 for a, b in spine_edges if v in (a, b)) <= 2 for e in spine_edges for v in e)}')
def cut_defect(cells, c, S1, S2):
    P = defaultdict(set); R = defaultdict(set)
    for x in cells: P[x[c]].add(proj(x, S1)); R[x[c]].add(proj(x, S2))

rows = []
for c in range(8):
    comp = r2lib.components(EDGES8, {c}, nodes=8)

    for v, root in comp.items(): groups[root].append(v)
    parts = sorted(sorted(g) for g in groups.values())

    else:

part = {i: 'A' for i in A_IDX}; part[Q_IDX] = 'Q'; part.update({i: 'B' for i in B_IDX})

fut = defaultdict(set)

O = {r2lib.src(c) for c in L9}

print(f'   split (k−q, q−g): {dict(sorted(split.items()))} | table is its own transpose: {all(split[(i,j)]==split[(j,i)] for i in range(3) for j in range(3))}')
pure1 = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i > 0 and j == 0); pure2 = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i == 0 and j > 0); both = sum(v for (i, j), v in split.items() if i > 0 and j > 0)

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"MC L1312 (28 chars): ### Past, present and future
MC L1314 (2788 chars): **Reading the constraint tree as past — change — future (§10.2) has an arithmetic, and it is not the arithmetic of three free things. Treated as independent the three parts overcount by 130 %: |A| × |Q| × |B| = 33 × 4 × 17 = 2,244 against |Λ| = 976, a defect of 1,268. Conditioned on the transfer they separate exactly, defect zero — but the balance is not special to the transfer. Every two-sided cut of the tree gives it: ℓ, q, f and g, all defect zero, so the two-body separation (§12.6.1) presents the factorisation as though the transfer did the work when the tree does it, and q is distinguished only by which two things it separates. And the reason it is exactly four is the tree: deleting a coordinate splits the constraint graph into two components precisely when that coordinate is an internal vertex of degree two, and n, e and 2S are leaves while k has degree three, so ℓ, q, f and g are the caterpillar's four internal degree-two vertices and the only two-sided cuts that exist. The future is never a value: of 97 (past, present) pairs none determines a single future — futures per pair run 5, median 10, maximum 17 — and for each value of the present every past gives the same future set. At present 0 there are 33 distinct pasts and one future set of 5; at present 1, 33 pasts and one set of 10; at present 2, 23 pasts and one set of 15; at present 3, 8 pasts and one set of 17. The future is conditionally independent of the past given the present, a Markov property exact at every value: the past constrains only which presents are reachable, and having spent that it has spent everything. The dependence is monotone and opposed, the future set nesting increasing 5 ⊂ 10 ⊂ 15 ⊂ 17 while the past set nests decreasing 33 ⊇ 33 ⊇ 23 ⊇ 8, and the bracket is saturated — at every present the admissible future is the full interval between its own extremes, E(X) = 0 read on the target end. The tick decomposes: over the 1,169 composable cells the clock k − g ticks 0, 1 or 2 across 389, 540 and 240 cells, and k − g = (k − q) + (q − g) has two sources, something not removed and something removed but not placed, 350 against 350 pure with 80 in both, the split table its own transpose — (0,1) = 270 against (1,0) = 270, (0,2) = 80 against (2,0) = 80. Irreversibility has two independent sources contributing identically: one a choice not taken, the other a capacity that could not receive, and the index weights them the same. And Pauli is a minority partner — g's ceiling is fixed by counting in 60.2 % of composable cells, tied in 29.5 % and by shell capacity in only 10.3 % — so the arrow of time in this object is overwhelmingly a counting phenomenon. That the shape is a path and not a triangle is the exactness ⇒ not-a-triangle theorem (§12.11.0.8), proved separately.**

# READ-ch12l — Phase R2, main volume §12.11.0.8 "Past, present and future — a path, not a triangle" (chat 75)

Member The_Method_1_6-2.md (BUILD90 main, md5 4aef772b…), L2842–L2897 (56 lines, none over 400 characters; §12.11.0.9 opens at L2898), read in full against each cited section (§10.2 L2032–2074 with the reading at L2038; §12.6.1 L2359–2400 with the table at L2367–2373 and the enumeration at L2398; §18.4.1 L4999 with the three-body passage at L5148–5155; §12.9 L2460–2523 with the binding rates at L2472), the Register (357 at R L1303–1305, 408 at R L1519–1521, 316 at R L1175–1177), the Mathematical Compendium's mirror entry (MC L1312–1318), the banked instruments r2-ch12f (the 389 sites, the 182,719 : 9,331 split) and r2-ch12i (Λ₉′'s closure), the rebuilt tower (tower-2.py, c0bce27a…) and the segment instrument r2-ch12l.py (r2lib by path; every claim on all 976 cells of Λ₈ and all 1,654 cells of Λ₉). Pointers: r2-tools resolves §10.2, §12.6.1, Register 408, §18.4.1, §12.9 and Register 357 to headings; the lowercase `register 316` at L2865 (missed by its case-sensitive regex) resolves by hand to R L1175 and is counted by register_cites.py, whose regex is case-insensitive. Census rows in range: 1064, 1065 (both C9), closed in CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch12l.tsv.

## A. Deviations (both texts)

**12l-01 · L2863–2864 (with MC L1314, L1318) — "treewidth 2 gives an envelope" is not what §18.4.1 says, and the tower's own treewidth-2 index closes exactly; the inference "Λ's exactness is a proof that the three parts are not a triangle" does not go through.** PRINTED L2862–2864: `**The shape is a path.** Two edges, past ↔ present and present ↔ future, and no past–future edge — treewidth 1. By §18.4.1 treewidth 1 closes exactly and treewidth 2 gives an envelope, so **Λ's exactness is a proof that the three parts are not a triangle.**` MC L1314 (end): `That the shape is a path and not a triangle is the exactness ⇒ not-a-triangle theorem (§12.11.0.8), proved separately.` — MC L1318 `Proved — M §12.11.0.8`. SOURCE §18.4.1 L5148–5155: `The interaction graph of n bodies is K_n: two bodies give one edge, treewidth 1, a tree — Λ's own shape, which §7.1 says three central results follow from. Three bodies give a triangle, treewidth 2. And superposition is a **sum**: φ(a,b) = a + b breaks 400 meets where φ(a) = a breaks none. The three-body problem carries all three of §12.11.2's excluded forms at once … so it is the maximal case of what Chapter 18 forbids, and the book's prediction is envelope precision only.` — the envelope there is derived from the triangle *and* the sum (the excluded forms), not from treewidth alone, and the treewidth-1 half is attributed to §7.1, not stated as §18.4.1's own. MEASURED (r2-ch12l, and r2-ch12i's banked golden): Λ₉′ = Λ₉ ∩ {2S′ ≤ 2f+1} has the triangle f–g–2S′ (3 edges among the three, treewidth 2) and closes exactly — join leaves 0, meet leaves 0 on all 2,436,721 ordered pairs, E(Λ₉′) = 0. So "treewidth 2 gives an envelope", read as closure, is false of the tower's one cycle row, and modus tollens from E(Λ) = 0 to "not a triangle" is unsound. (Read instead as the Markov property, the premise fares no better: READ-ch12k C records that on the (g, G) index, whose constraint graph is not a tree — 12k-02 — the chain (n,e) ⊥ (2S,2S′) | (k,G) holds with 0 failures, so exact conditional independence at a cut does not certify that the cut separates.) The conclusion itself is true and measured directly: the constraint tree has one A–Q edge (k–q), one Q–B edge (q–g) and no A–B edge, so the quotient on {past, present, future} is a path (treewidth 1). What is wrong is the route: the "theorem" the MC names is the direct measurement's conclusion attached to a premise the tower refutes. For R3: L2863–2864 (main), MC L1314's final sentence and its "Proved" status at L1318 (MC segment).

**12l-02 · L2891 (with MC L1314) — "two independent sources" is not independence in the sense this section itself uses at L2877.** PRINTED L2891–2892: `**Irreversibility has two independent sources contributing identically.** One is a choice not taken; the other a capacity that could not receive. The index weights them the same.` — the same sentence at MC L1314. The section's own standard is the exact count test (L2877 `conditionally independent … exact at every value`, verified below with 0 failures). MEASURED (r2-ch12l, all 1,169 composable cells): the two sources k − q and q − g are *dependent* — the exact count test N(i,j)·N = N(i,·)·N(·,j) fails on 9 of 9 cells of the (k−q, q−g) table; N(1,1) = 80 against 104.8 under independence; mutual information 0.109 bits. "Contributing identically" is exact: the table is its own transpose and the two marginals are both [739, 350, 80]. Word-level (the C9 class); the neighbouring measured sentence uses the word technically. For R3: L2891 and MC L1314.

**12l-03 · layout.** L2871–2875 column-dump table (3 gaps); L2877–2879 and L2891–2892 four-space paragraphs render as code. Production.

## B. Verified (all MEASURED unless marked; r2-ch12l.py)

- L2843 §10.2 (L2032) resolves; L2038 reads `The constraint tree *is* past — change — future, read left to right.`
- L2846–2847: |A| (n,ℓ,k,2S) = 33, |Q| = 4, |B| (e,f,g) = 17; 33 · 4 · 17 = 2,244 against |Λ₈| = 976, defect 1,268 = 129.9 % ("130%"); conditioned on q, Σ_q |A_q|·|B_q| − 976 = 0 with A_q = 33, 33, 23, 8 and B_q = 5, 10, 15, 17 (cross-sections 165, 330, 345, 136 — §12.6.1 L2367–2373, L2383, L2398 carry the same figures).
- L2849–2852: the constraint tree of Λ₈ is EDGES9 without the 2S′ edge — n–ℓ, ℓ–k, k–q, k–2S, e–f, f–g, q–g — a tree (7 edges on 8 vertices, connected). Deleting ℓ, q, f or g leaves exactly two components and the factorisation across those two components has defect 0 at each of the four. §12.6.1 (L2359) resolves and factorises at q only (its table L2367–2373; L2398 `verified against enumeration at every *q*`), which is what L2850–2852 says of it.
- L2854–2860: degrees n 1, ℓ 2, k 3, q 2, e 1, f 2, g 2, 2S 1; leaves n, e, 2S each leave one component; k leaves three ({n,ℓ}, {q,e,f,g}, {2S}); removing the leaves leaves the path ℓ–k–q–g–f (a caterpillar); the internal degree-two vertices are exactly ℓ, q, f, g and they are exactly the two-sided cuts. Register 408 (R L1521) `THE FOUR TWO-SIDED CUTS ARE THE CATERPILLAR'S FOUR INTERNAL DEGREE-TWO VERTICES … The list was right and unexplained` agrees; the list it explains is Register 357's `the balance holds at every two-sided cut, not only at q` (R L1305), which gives no reason — L2860's `never said why` is true of the record (census 1064).
- L2862–2863: quotient on {A, Q, B}: A–Q 1 (k–q), Q–B 1 (q–g), A–B 0 — a path on three vertices, treewidth 1 (the conclusion of 12l-01, established by this measurement rather than by the printed route). L2865 `register 316` (R L1177) states the three-body price: K_n a triangle at three bodies, superposition a sum, E > 0.
- L2867–2868: (past, present) pairs 97 = 33 + 33 + 23 + 8; 0 of 97 determine a single future (census 1065); futures per pair min 5, median 10, max 17.
- L2871–2875 the table: at q = 0, 1, 2, 3 — distinct pasts 33, 33, 23, 8; distinct future sets 1, 1, 1, 1; |future| 5, 10, 15, 17.
- L2877–2879: (n,ℓ,k,2S) ⊥ (e,f,g) | q is exact on Λ₈ — 976 product cells, 0 count-test failures (r2lib.ci_sets).
- L2881–2882: B_0 ⊂ B_1 ⊂ B_2 ⊂ B_3 strictly (5 ⊂ 10 ⊂ 15 ⊂ 17); A_0 = A_1 ⊇ A_2 ⊇ A_3 (33 ⊇ 33 ⊇ 23 ⊇ 8), the first inclusion an equality as the printed ⊇ allows.
- L2882–2884: at every q both extremes lo = (1,0,0) and hi = (3,1,q) lie in B_q, and B_q equals the interval {b ∈ B : lo ≤ b ≤ hi} of the 17-element target set (5, 10, 15, 17 of 17) — saturated; each B_q and B itself close exactly (join leaves 0, meet leaves 0): `E(X) = 0 read on the target end`.
- L2886: composable cells (target a source object) 1,169 of 1,654 — equal to the cells with g ≥ 1 (485 non-composable); the tick k − g over them is 0 : 1 : 2 = 389 : 540 : 240 (over all 1,654 cells the maximum is 3, on non-composable cells, so the printed scope is the right one). The 389 tick-0 cells are exactly r2-ch12f's 389 cells on a composition cycle (source and target in one of the 3 SCCs; set identity True) and the 389 object edges with a reverse edge reproduce — the DEFERRED item's L2886 site; the 182,719 : 9,331 path-pair split has no site in this section (its L2909/L2915 sites are §12.11.0.9's).
- L2887–2889: the (k−q, q−g) table is (0,0) 389, (0,1) 270, (1,0) 270, (0,2) 80, (2,0) 80, (1,1) 80 — its own transpose; pure k−q 350, pure q−g 350, both 80; tick 1 = 540 = (0,1)+(1,0), tick 2 = 240 = (0,2)+(2,0)+(1,1). Register 357's `430 against 430` (R L1305) is the same table counted as any-active (350 + 80 on each side); both texts reproduce, they count differently.
- L2894–2895: over the 1,169 composable cells g's ceiling min(4f+2, q) is fixed by counting (q < 4f+2) in 704 = 60.2 %, tied (q = 4f+2) in 345 = 29.5 %, by shell capacity (4f+2 < q) in 120 = 10.3 %. L2896 §12.9 (L2460) resolves; the advance statement is L2472 `The most active constraint is the coupling; the least is the Pauli bound` (binding rates g≤q 35.6 %, q≤k 33.0 %, g ≤ 4f+2 4.9 %), a different population and question (which constraint binds on §12.9's intervals, not whose bound is g's ceiling on composable cells), carrying 12c-03/04; consistent in direction, not the same figure. Register 357 (R L1305) carries the section's four headline claims.
- MC L1314–1318 mirrors the section: every figure there (130 %, 33 × 4 × 17 = 2,244, 1,268, 97, 5/10/15/17, 33/33/23/8, 1,169, 389/540/240, 350/350/80, 270/270/80/80, 60.2/29.5/10.3 %) reproduces; its scope line L1316 names the caps (3, 3, 1, 3, 1), the tower's.
- Census 1064 (C9 "never", L2860) and 1065 (C9 "never", L2867): not defects — see CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch12l.tsv.

## C. Incidental

- The "coordinate order" cut that L2858 contrasts with the tree cut is nonzero at three of the four vertices — before | after in (n,ℓ,k,q,e,f,g,2S): ℓ 0, q 300, f 1,268, g 300 — because 2S falls on the wrong side of q and e on the wrong side of f; the tree cut is what makes all four zero, which is the point of L2858–2859.
- L2883's "full interval between its own extremes" holds in the target lattice B, not in the ambient box: the Z³ boxes [lo, hi] hold 6, 12, 18, 24 triples against |B_q| = 5, 10, 15, 17, the excess being (e, f) = (1, 1) triples that are not targets at all.
- L2867 `futures per pair run 5, median 10, maximum 17` — "run 5" reads as "min 5"; prose, not a figure (MC L1314 repeats it).
- L2865 `register 316` lowercase: one of some fifty lowercase `register NNN` sites in the main volume (house style); register_cites.py counts them ((?i)), r2-tools' pointer regex does not — resolve lowercase pointers by hand in every segment.
- Register 357 and the main/MC text count the tick's sources differently (430 any-active against 350 pure + 80 both); a reader comparing the two must add — for the Register expansions line after the review, not a defect.
- r2-ch12l.py's tree-cut factorisation (`cut_defect` over components) and ceiling census are reusable for §12.11.1's per-axis sections; the segment ran in under 5 s.

 If composition has a direction, the obvious question is what the other direction is. It is not a sign
 change — extending k, q and g below zero leaves the object closed and leaves the clock intact, because
 a negative occupancy is a *lower* one and not a reversed one.

 **The reversal is a different object.** Exchange the two ends of Λ₉ — (n,ℓ,k,2S) ↔ (e,f,g,2S′), the
 transfer unchanged. Recomputed here:

 **The reversed index is a lawful closed index of the same size, and it is not Λ₉.** That is §11.8's
 failure of self-duality read temporally: both are lawful and simply not the same object.

 **The intersection is where time has no direction.** Every one of its 389 cells satisfies **g = q = k**
 — total transfer, nothing retained and nothing lost — and that is exactly the set of morphisms
 carrying a reverse. It closes at E = 0, it factorises over its own transfer, and it is a **groupoid**:
 every object carries an identity and every morphism a two-sided inverse. §12.11.0.1's cycles were
 confined to level sets of occupancy with every step conservative; conservative is g = q and the
 level-set condition is k = g. **The intersection is that condition stated as an object rather than as
 a property of paths**, and it is 23.5% of Λ₉.

 **2,857 further cells** — §16.8.4's amplification, priced.

 A structure holding both directions of time is not available at any price this index recognises. What

# READ-ch12m — Phase R2, main volume §12.11.0.9 "Two indices, and the one that does not exist" (chat 75)

Member The_Method_1_6-2.md (BUILD90 main, md5 4aef772b…), L2898–L2931 (34 lines, none over 400 characters; §12.11.0.10 opens at L2932), read in full against each cited section (§11.8 L2275–2303 with the self-duality statement at L2276 and the dual σ at L2285; §12.11.0.1 L2577–2628; §16.8.4 L4691–4716 with the amplification at L4703, L4710, L4716), the Register (350 at R L1283–1285), the Mathematical Compendium's mirror entry (MC L1332–1340; L1336 defines E as the iterated join-and-meet closure to a fixed point), the banked r2-ch12f (the 389 cycle cells, the object edges with a reverse) and r2-ch12i (Λ₉'s closure on 2,735,716 ordered pairs), the rebuilt tower (tower-2.py, c0bce27a…) and the segment instrument r2-ch12m.py (r2lib by path; every claim on all 1,654 cells of Λ₉, all 1,654 of rev(Λ₉), the 389 of the intersection and the 2,919 of the union, closure on every ordered pair, chunked, with the chunked routine checked against r2lib.closure). Pointers: all four resolve to headings and to the claims cited. Census rows in range: none (CENSUS-CLOSURES-ch12m.tsv is a header).

## A. Deviations (both texts)

**12m-01 · L2899–2901 (with MC L1334) — the sign-extension result has no recoverable construction, and under the tower's own ranges it is vacuous; under the one extension that admits negative cells the object does not close.** PRINTED L2899–2901: `It is not a sign change — extending k, q and g below zero leaves the object closed and leaves the clock intact, because a negative occupancy is a *lower* one and not a reversed one.` MC L1334: `extending k, q and g below zero leaves the object closed and the clock intact, a negative occupancy being a lower one and not a reversed one.` SOURCE: no figure is printed at either site, Register 350 (R L1285) does not record the extension, and no Register or MC site names its ranges (grep of all volumes for "below zero", "negative occupancy", "sign change": these two sites only). MEASURED (r2-ch12m): with the lower bounds of k, q and g lowered to 0, −1 or −3 and every other range as tower-2.py prints them (2S ∈ [0, k], g ∈ [0, min(4f+2, q)], 2S′ ∈ [0, g]), the object gains the 25 cells at k = q = g = 0 and **no cell with k, q or g below zero** — 1,679 cells at every lower bound below 1, closure 0/0, steps raising k 0 — because the spin ranges are empty below zero: the extension the sentence describes admits nothing. Under the one reading that does admit negative cells (2S ∈ [0, |k|], 2S′ ∈ [0, |g|]) the object has 3,179 cells at lower bound −1 (1,500 negative) and **776,250 failing joins** (meet 0); at −2, 6,374 cells and 7,892,050 failing joins — not closed. The clock (no step raising k) survives under every reading, trivially, since g ≤ q ≤ k is kept. The printed claim is a computation without a population, and the two populations that can be reconstructed give "vacuous" and "false" respectively. Class: printed measurement lacking a recoverable population (READ-ch11's class). For R3: L2899–2901 and MC L1334.

**12m-02 · layout.** L2906–2910 column-dump table (3–4 gaps); L2926–2927 four-space paragraph renders as code. Production.

## B. Verified (all MEASURED unless marked; r2-ch12m.py)

- L2903–2904 the reversal: rev(c) = (e, f, g, q, n, ℓ, k, 2S′, 2S) in Λ₉'s slots is an involution on cells; rev(Λ₉) has 1,654 cells and rev(Λ₉) ≠ Λ₉ (L2912 `it is not Λ₉`).
- L2906–2910 the table: Λ₉ forward 1,654 cells, 0 join failures, 0 meet failures, E = 0; rev(Λ₉) 1,654, 0, 0, E = 0; Λ₉ ∩ rev(Λ₉) 389, 0, 0, E = 0; Λ₉ ∪ rev(Λ₉) 2,919 = 2 · 1,654 − 389 cells, **360,000 failing joins and 470,625 failing meets counted as unordered pairs** (my ordered-pair count is exactly twice, 720,000 and 941,250, of 8,520,561 ordered pairs; a pair with itself never fails), E = 2,857 cells added by the iterated closure (fixed point in 2 iterations, closure size 5,776) — and the same 2,857 as the distinct missing joins and meets after one step, so MC L1336's "iterated … not a single projection" and the one-step count coincide here. L2923 `830,625 failing pairs` = 360,000 + 470,625.
- L2912–2913 §11.8 (L2275) resolves: L2276 `A rank polynomial is palindromic if and only if the poset is self-dual`, L2285 the dual σ(x) = max − x; Λ₉ is not self-dual under σ (σ(Λ₉) ≠ Λ₉), which is the failure §11.8 states.
- L2915–2916: all 389 intersection cells satisfy g = q = k, and they are exactly the 389 cells of Λ₉ with g = q = k; they are exactly the cells whose (source, target) object pair has the reverse edge (r2-ch12f's 389) and exactly r2-ch12f's 389 cells on a composition cycle — the DEFERRED item's L2909/L2915 sites; the 182,719 : 9,331 path-pair split has no site in this section either (READ-ch12l B for L2886).
- L2917: the intersection closes (0/0) and factorises over its own transfer (Σ_q |A_q||B_q| − 389 = 0).
- L2917–2918 groupoid, under r2-ch12e's composition (b∘a when tgt(a) = src(b), composite (src(a), min(q_a, q_b), tgt(b))): the intersection's objects are all 33 source objects; each carries its identity cell (the 33 identity cells of Λ₉, src = tgt, all lie in the intersection); every one of the 389 cells has rev(c) in the intersection as a two-sided inverse with both composites the identities of its ends; all 4,887 composable pairs compose inside the intersection; composition is associative. MC L1334's `every one of its 33 objects carrying an identity` agrees.
- L2918–2920: on every cycle cell g = q (conservative) and k = g (level set) — §12.11.0.1's two conditions, and the intersection is the set they define.
- L2921: 389 / 1,654 = 23.5 %.
- L2923–2924 §16.8.4 (L4691) resolves; L4703 `insert one — amplifies, always — minimum 59`, L4710 `the amplification is governed by the fibre the widened bound admits`, L4716 `A forger must therefore supply the whole amplified set, and its size is computable` — the amplification the sentence prices.
- L2926–2927 three of four positions close (E = 0) and the union does not (E = 2,857). Register 350 (R L1285) carries the section: reversal lawful, closed, same size, not Λ₉; 389 at g = q = k, a groupoid; union E = 2,857.
- MC L1334–1340 mirrors the section; every figure there (1,654, 389, 33, 23.5 %, 2,919, 360,000, 470,625, 2,857) reproduces under the readings above.

## C. Incidental

- The table's failing-pair columns count unordered pairs while r2-ch12i's banked closure (and r2lib.closure) count ordered pairs; the print does not say which, and for the three zero rows it cannot be told — the union row fixes it. A reader recomputing with r2lib will get double the printed figures.
- §11.8's failure of self-duality and the end-exchange are different facts: rev(Λ₉) ≠ σ(Λ₉) (they share 144 cells); L2912–2913's "read temporally" is an analogy between two distinct non-identities, not one fact.
- Lowering the occupancy bounds to 0 (not below) adds exactly the 25 cells at k = q = g = 0 — the empty-occupancy cells the tower excludes by k ≥ 1 — and the object stays closed; this is the only lawful "extension" the printed ranges allow.
- 12l-01's route is also stated in the previous entry's prior-art line, MC L1330: `That E(Λ) = 0 therefore proves Λ's past–present–future graph is a tree`, reading Freuder's sufficiency (width one + consistency ⇒ globally consistent) as necessity; Λ₉′ is the counterexample. For the MC segment, with MC L1314/L1318.
- r2-ch12m.py's `closure_chunked` and `fixed_point` (200-row chunks, 9 int64 coordinates) run the 2,919-cell union in under 40 s within 4 GB; lift into r2lib when a later segment needs closure on more than ~2,000 cells.

 The tower is reported in six places under six aspects. This is all of it, computed in one pass.

  Λ₉′       9     1,561    0        27,648   5.65%    —                + 2S′ ≤ 2f+1          exact · composes
  Λ₁₀      10     2,535    0       110,592   2.29%    v                2S′ ≤ v ≤ g           exact · does not compose
  Λ₁₁      11    13,585    0       663,552   2.05%    2J_c             2J_c ≤ φ̂(k)           envelope · does not compose
  Λ₁₂      12    70,905    0     5,308,416   1.34%    K                2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f_max    envelope · does not compose
  Λ₁₃      13   199,130    0    47,775,744   0.42%    2J               |2J − 2K| ≤ 1         envelope · does not compose

 **Every stage closes.** E = 0 at all seven, tested against every cell of the ambient box and not by
 pairs — forty-seven million cells at Λ₁₃, per register 249. Closure is the one property the tower
 never spends.

 **Everything else falls monotonically.** Fill runs 14.12% down to 0.42%: each coordinate multiplies
 the box faster than it multiplies the object, so **the surplus §11.1.1 measures at seven bits per cell
 in Λ₈ grows at every step**. The tower is not a refinement that sharpens; it is a refinement that
 admits more room and fills less of it.

 **And the two gradings part company at different heights.** Composition is lost at Λ₁₀ and exactness
 at Λ₁₁, so there is a stage — Λ₁₀ — that is exact and does not compose, and no stage that composes
 without being exact. Register 315.

# r2-ch12n.py — Phase R2, main §12.11.0.10 "Every Λ in one table" (L2932–2956), chat 75.
# Every row of the tower table re-measured from tower-2.py (by path, through r2lib): cells, ambient box (product of realised
# coordinate ranges), fill, closure E, composition; then the fill's monotonicity, the box-versus-object ratios, and §11.1.1's
# surplus (bits carried = |J(Λ_d)| = lattice length, minus log2 cells) at every stage. Closure: pairwise on every ordered pair
# for Λ₈, Λ₉, Λ₉′, Λ₁₀, Λ₁₁ (r2lib.closure's semantics, chunked); for Λ₁₂ and Λ₁₃ the exact fibre-interval criterion, measured
# on ALL cells: each stage is Λ_{d−1} fibred by an interval [lo, hi] of the new coordinate whose bounds depend on one earlier
# coordinate u (verified on every cell), and given Λ_{d−1} closed, Λ_d is closed iff for every realised pair (u, u′):
# lo(max) ≤ max(lo u, lo u′), max(hi u, hi u′) ≤ hi(max), lo(min) ≤ min(lo u, lo u′), min(hi u, hi u′) ≤ hi(min). Deterministic.
import importlib.util, os, math
from collections import defaultdict
import numpy as np
H = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
s = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('r2lib', os.path.join(H, 'r2lib.py')); r2lib = importlib.util.module_from_spec(s); s.loader.exec_module(r2lib); T = r2lib.load_tower()

def closure_chunked(X, chunk=100):
    A = np.array(X, dtype=np.int64); n = len(A); base = A.min(axis=0); rad = A.max(axis=0) - base + 1
    w = np.cumprod(np.concatenate(([1], rad[:-1]))); key = np.sort((A - base) @ w); jl = ml = 0
    for i in range(0, n, chunk):
        Ai = A[i:i+chunk, None, :]; Aj = A[None, :, :]
        J = ((np.maximum(Ai, Aj) - base) @ w).ravel(); Mt = ((np.minimum(Ai, Aj) - base) @ w).ravel()
        jl += int((~np.isin(J, key)).sum()); ml += int((~np.isin(Mt, key)).sum())
    return n * n, jl, ml

def box(X):

Register 249 (R L985) records the box-exhaustive test to 47,775,744 cells; this chat reproduces E = 0 by the two routes above, not by that one (C).
- L2936–2942 the "new coordinate / bounded by" column is tower-2.py's stage definitions (r2-ch12e.out's axes line): 2S′ ≤ g; Λ₉′ adds 2S′ ≤ 2f+1; 2S′ ≤ v ≤ g; 2J_c ≤ φ̂(k) with φ̂ = {1: 3, 2: 4, 3: 5}; 2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f_max with f_max = 1; |2J − 2K| ≤ 1 (with the spin floor 2J ≥ 0 that tower-2.py applies at 2K = 0).

## C. Incidental

- L2949's "so": the fill's decrease is the *box* surplus log₂(box/cells) (2.82 → 4.06 → 5.45 → 5.61 → 6.23 → 7.91 bits), while "seven bits per cell" is §11.1.1's *generator* surplus (|J| − log₂ cells). Both grow at every step, so the sentence is true, but it names one quantity and argues from the other.
- Register 249's box-exhaustive closure (every box cell, 47.7 M at Λ₁₃) is not reproduced in this container; E = 0 is reproduced pairwise to Λ₁₁ and by the exact fibre criterion above it. No disagreement with the record.
- The exact/envelope half of the grading column (exactness "lost at Λ₁₁") is a provenance classification with no computation behind it here; §12.11.3.1 (L3409–3461) carries it with 12j-01's "three values, not two" (DEFERRED) — the two-valued column here may be the site that line was written against.
- L2933 `reported in six places under six aspects` is not testable from the sentence (the six are not named); the tower's cell counts appear at many more than six sites (r2-tools: 199,130 at 13 main sites).
- L2942's `|2J − 2K| ≤ 1` reads as symmetric; tower-2.py floors 2J at 0, which only bites at 2K = 0 (2J ∈ {0, 1}); the box count 47,775,744 = 9 · 5,308,416 is on the realised range 0…8 either way.
- r2-ch12n.py's `length()` (greedy cover chain, exact on any finite lattice with a bottom) and `fibre_check`/`criterion` are reusable for §12.11.1's per-axis sections and for any closure claim above Λ₁₁; the instrument runs in about 60 s, the Λ₁₁ pairwise closure being 40 s of it.

### 12.11.0.11 The fourteenth axis, and what can be said about it from inside
 The tower stops at thirteen because the physics stopped being supplied, not because the construction
 did. **What lies beyond can be bounded without being built**, and the bound is a bracket rather than a
 value.

  D    cells      ambient box     fill     bits carried   needed   surplus
   8      976           6,912   14.12%            12.75     9.93      2.82
   9    1,654          27,648    5.98%            14.75    10.69      4.06
  10    2,535         110,592    2.29%            16.75    11.31      5.45
  11   13,585        663,552     2.05%            19.34    13.73      5.61
  12   70,905       5,308,416    1.34%            22.34    16.11      6.23
  13  199,130      47,775,744    0.42%            25.51    17.60      7.91

 **Fill falls at every step and surplus rises at every step**, and the first of those is a law rather
 than a pattern. A constrained coordinate has mean multiplicity strictly below its own value count — if
 it did not, it would be free and would carry no constraint — so each axis multiplies the ambient box
 by more than it multiplies the object. Fill is therefore monotone decreasing **by construction**, and
 bounded below by zero.

    **The sequence converges. Its limit lies in [0, 0.42%]. That the limit is zero does not
    follow.**

 Monotone and bounded gives convergence, which is a deduction. The ratios stage to stage are 0.424,
 0.383, 0.893, 0.652 and 0.312 — not themselves monotone — so nothing in the construction forbids them
 approaching one and the limit settling above zero. **§22.1.2's rule applies to the tower's own tail:
 the existence of the limit comes from the law and survives; its value would come from the pattern and
 does not.**

 **This is what the index can say about a coordinate it does not have.** It cannot name the fourteenth
 axis — §32.1.4 shows ℛ never produces a coordinate — but it can bound the *direction*: an object that
 occupies less and less of its own ambient box while carrying more and more surplus. In the limit the
 index would be a vanishing fraction of the space it is written in and would defend itself with
 unbounded redundancy. **Whether that limit is a null or merely a small number is exactly the question
 the construction leaves open**, and leaving it open is the correct answer rather than a gap.

 **And a null is definable in this language, which is worth stating where the tower ends.** The empty
 index satisfies every criterion in this book: ℛ(∅) = ∅, so E(∅) = 0 and it is closed; Q(∅) = ∅, so it
 is COMPLETE by P19, which is strictly stronger. It has zero join-irreducibles and takes zero bits.
 **E(X) = 0 is therefore necessary for completeness and not sufficient for content** — every closure
 test in this book passes on nothing at all. What distinguishes Λ from the empty index is not closure
 but |J(Λ)| = 17 and its seven bits of surplus. Register 333.

import importlib.util, os, math
import numpy as np
H = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
s = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('r2lib', os.path.join(H, 'r2lib.py')); r2lib = importlib.util.module_from_spec(s); s.loader.exec_module(r2lib); T = r2lib.load_tower()

stages = [(d, T.STAGES[d]()) for d in range(8, 14)]

2999	### 12.11.0.12 How an index enters a larger index, and what it looks like from there
  3000	 §12.11.0.9 bounds the direction beyond thirteen. This is the other question: **what happens to Λ when
  3001	 it becomes a coordinate of something bigger.** All three answers are computed, and none of them
  3002	 requires the larger index to be built.
  3003	
  3004	 **It enters as a chain, and it enters small.** A coordinate must be totally ordered and Λ₁₃ is a
  3005	 lattice, so the only chain-valued function ℛ accepts on it is its rank. 199,130 cells become **44
  3006	 rank values**: 17.60 bits collapse to 5.46, a compression of 4,526 to 1, with **12.14 bits per cell
  3007	 lost.** Thirty-one per cent of the object survives the promotion and the rest is not representable as
  3008	 a coordinate at all. Structurally the result is the same kind of thing as dimension 1 of Λ, which is a
  3009	 chain of three — so an index can be an axis of another, at that price.
  3010	
  3011	 **A coarse coordinate is a branching node.** At Λ₉ the rank chain has 21 values and the fibres beneath
  3012	 them run from 1 cell to **185**. One point above stands for up to a hundred and eighty-five below, and
  3013	 nothing in the coordinate distinguishes them.
  3014	
  3015	 **And composition, seen from above, stops being a map and becomes a bracket.** Λ₉ composes: 41,682
  3016	 pairs, closed and associative. Reduced to rank there are 264 distinct (rank a, rank b) inputs, and
  3017	 **only 17% of them determine a single output rank.** The worst spread is **twelve** possible output
  3018	 ranks from one input pair; the composite's rank lies in [3, 23], narrowed by the inputs and not fixed
  3019	 by them.
  3020	
  3021	    **From one coordinate up, a transition is not a function of its inputs. It is an interval.**
  3022	
  3023	 That is §22.1's bracket arriving unbidden, one dimension higher, and it is the clearest statement in
  3024	 this book of what coarsening costs: not error, but resolution — the deduction stays valid and stops
  3025	 being sharp.
  3026	
  3027	 **What this does not show.** The branching is *inside* the index. Those 185 cells are cells of Λ₉,
  3028	 states of the same object. What the collapse loses is resolution, not access to anything else, and
  3029	 ignorance about this index is not evidence of another. **Every branch terminates in a cell of Λ₉.**

### 12.11.0.12 How an index enters a larger index, and what it looks like from there
 §12.11.0.9 bounds the direction beyond thirteen. This is the other question: **what happens to Λ when
 it becomes a coordinate of something bigger.** All three answers are computed, and none of them
 requires the larger index to be built.

 **It enters as a chain, and it enters small.** A coordinate must be totally ordered and Λ₁₃ is a
 lattice, so the only chain-valued function ℛ accepts on it is its rank. 199,130 cells become **44
 rank values**: 17.60 bits collapse to 5.46, a compression of 4,526 to 1, with **12.14 bits per cell
 lost.** Thirty-one per cent of the object survives the promotion and the rest is not representable as
 a coordinate at all. Structurally the result is the same kind of thing as dimension 1 of Λ, which is a
 chain of three — so an index can be an axis of another, at that price.

 **A coarse coordinate is a branching node.** At Λ₉ the rank chain has 21 values and the fibres beneath
 them run from 1 cell to **185**. One point above stands for up to a hundred and eighty-five below, and
 nothing in the coordinate distinguishes them.

 **And composition, seen from above, stops being a map and becomes a bracket.** Λ₉ composes: 41,682
 pairs, closed and associative. Reduced to rank there are 264 distinct (rank a, rank b) inputs, and
 **only 17% of them determine a single output rank.** The worst spread is **twelve** possible output
 ranks from one input pair; the composite's rank lies in [3, 23], narrowed by the inputs and not fixed
 by them.

    **From one coordinate up, a transition is not a function of its inputs. It is an interval.**

 That is §22.1's bracket arriving unbidden, one dimension higher, and it is the clearest statement in
 this book of what coarsening costs: not error, but resolution — the deduction stays valid and stops
 being sharp.

 **What this does not show.** The branching is *inside* the index. Those 185 cells are cells of Λ₉,
 states of the same object. What the collapse loses is resolution, not access to anything else, and
 ignorance about this index is not evidence of another. **Every branch terminates in a cell of Λ₉.**
 Register 334.
